claim: A total of 519 proteins were identified over the 73 colony and 40 single-individual trophallactic fluid samples analyzed.
source: Over the 73 colony and 40 single-individual trophallactic fluid samples analyzed, a total of 519 proteins were identified (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript directly reports the number of proteins identified across all samples analyzed.

claim: Trophallactic fluid samples contained a set of 27 'core' trophallactic fluid proteins that were present in all samples regardless of life-cycle, life-stage or environmental conditions.
source: Trophallactic fluid samples contained a set of 27 'core' trophallactic fluid proteins that were present in all samples regardless of life-cycle, life-stage or environmental conditions.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of core proteins present in all samples.

claim: Fifty-seven percent of the 519 proteins observed were present in less than half of the samples.
source: Fifty-seven percent of the 519 proteins, we observed were present in less than half of the samples.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage based on analysis of the protein dataset.

claim: The number of proteins identified for a given sample correlated with trophallactic fluid sample volume.
source: The number of proteins identified for a given sample correlated with trophallactic fluid sample volume (Pearson correlation test p < 0.03, r = 0.24 for colony samples and p < 0.01, r = –0.40 for single-individual samples).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical correlation tests with p-values and correlation coefficients.

claim: Field-collected samples exhibited more variable proteomes than did lab-collected samples.
source: Field-collected samples exhibited more variable proteomes than did lab-collected samples (Figure 2b, gamma GLM posthoc p-values < 0.001, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison with p-values and references Figure 2b.

claim: Colonies that had been in the lab for more than one year showed less variable proteomes than did colonies that had been in the lab for only six months.
source: Further, colonies that had been in the lab for more than one year showed less variable proteomes than did colonies that had been in the lab for only six months (Figure 2b, gamma GLM z = −4.46, SE = 0.04, p < 0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results comparing proteome variability over time in lab.

claim: Foragers had fewer identified proteins in their trophallactic fluid than did nurses.
source: Foragers had fewer identified proteins in their trophallactic fluid than did nurses (Figure 2a, negative binomial z = 3.72, SE = 0.08, p = 0.005)
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison with test statistics and p-value.

claim: Young colonies prioritize direct carbohydrate processing.
source: We show that different stages of the colony life cycle circulate different types of proteins: young colonies prioritize direct carbohydrate processing; mature colonies prioritize accumulation and transmission of stored resources.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a finding based on proteomic analysis and functional enrichment.

claim: Mature colonies prioritize accumulation and transmission of stored resources.
source: We show that different stages of the colony life cycle circulate different types of proteins: young colonies prioritize direct carbohydrate processing; mature colonies prioritize accumulation and transmission of stored resources.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a finding based on proteomic analysis and functional enrichment.

claim: Colonies circulate proteins implicated in oxidative stress, ageing, and social insect caste determination.
source: Further, colonies circulate proteins implicated in oxidative stress, ageing, and social insect caste determination, potentially acting as superorganismal hormones.
evidence: The manuscript identifies these protein types in trophallactic fluid through proteomic analysis.

claim: Brood-caring individuals that are also closer to the queen in the social network (nurses) showed higher abundance of oxidative stress-related proteins.
source: Brood-caring individuals that are also closer to the queen in the social network (nurses) showed higher abundance of oxidative stress-related proteins.
evidence: The manuscript reports differential protein abundance between nurses and foragers.

claim: Trophallaxis behavior could provide a mechanism for distributed metabolism in social insect societies.
source: Thus, trophallaxis behavior could provide a mechanism for distributed metabolism in social insect societies.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this mechanism based on the observed protein distributions and functions.

claim: Social insect societies develop and function as a single unit instead of as competing individuals, as 'superorganisms' paralleling the development of multicellular organisms.
source: Some social groups have taken this coordination to a very high level: social insect societies develop and function as a single unit instead of as competing individuals, as 'superorganisms' paralleling the development of multicellular organisms as a single unit rather than as a set of competing cells (Johnson and Linksvayer, 2010; Boomsma and Gawne, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this concept.

claim: In superorganismal societies, reproductive queens and males function as the germline, and workers as the soma.
source: In these superorganismal societies, reproductive queens and males function as the germline, and workers as the soma.
evidence: The manuscript states this as an established concept in social insect biology.

claim: Workers can be further specialized and exhibit division of labor across different behavioral and morphological castes.
source: Similarly to different tissues in multicellular organisms, workers can be further specialized and exhibit division of labor across different behavioral and morphological castes (Bourke, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement.

claim: At the beginning of their adult life, workers specialize inside the nest as nurses focusing on brood care, and as they age, they switch to foraging outside of the nest.
source: At the beginning of their adult life, workers specialize inside the nest as nurses focusing on brood care, and as they age, they switch to foraging outside of the nest (Huang and Robinson, 1996).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this behavioral pattern.

claim: Young colonies have an initial growth phase where they solely produce one type of worker, and only later in their life cycle they may produce more specialized worker castes and finally, males and queens.
source: Young colonies have an initial growth phase where they solely produce one type of worker, and only later in their life cycle they may produce more specialized worker castes and finally, males and queens (Wilson, 1971).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this colony development pattern.

claim: In social Hymenoptera, determination of whether a female larva develops into a queen or a worker is controlled by intricate differences of gene expression of the same female genome, guided primarily by environmental factors, in particular nutrition and social cues, sometimes partially influenced by genetics.
source: In social Hymenoptera, determination of whether a female larva develops into a queen or a worker, and what kind of worker exactly, is controlled by intricate differences of gene expression of the same female genome, guided primarily by environmental factors, in particular nutrition and social cues, sometimes partially influenced by genetics (Wheeler, 1986; Anderson et al., 2008; Rajakumar et al., 2018; Schwander et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple published studies to support this mechanism of caste determination.

claim: Some social insect societies have developed a form of social circulatory system where nutrition and endogenously produced functional molecules, such as hormones, are transferred mouth-to-mouth from the foregut of one individual to another.
source: As a part of their social physiology, some social insect societies have developed a form of social circulatory system (Wheeler, 1928), where nutrition and endogenously produced functional molecules, such as hormones, are transferred mouth-to-mouth from the foregut of one individual to another (LeBoeuf et al., 2016; LeBoeuf et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this description of trophallaxis.

claim: Trophallactic fluid of ants and bees typically contains endogenous proteins involved in digestion, immune defense and developmental regulation.
source: Trophallactic fluid of ants and bees typically contains endogenous proteins involved in digestion, immune defense and developmental regulation (LeBoeuf et al., 2016), indicating that this fluid transmits more than food.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this characterization of trophallactic fluid composition.

claim: Molecular components transmitted through trophallaxis, namely juvenile hormone and juvenile hormone esterase-like proteins, have been shown to influence the development of ant larvae.
source: Molecular components transmitted through trophallaxis, namely juvenile hormone and juvenile hormone esterase-like proteins, have been shown to influence the development of ant larvae (LeBoeuf et al., 2016; LeBoeuf et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites published studies demonstrating this developmental influence.

claim: Social isolation changes the composition of trophallactic fluid.
source: The molecular functions of trophallactic fluid are still largely unstudied, but it is known, for example, that social isolation changes its composition (LeBoeuf et al., 2016), with some protein components of this fluid shifting with social environment.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this observation.

claim: For the Young vs. Mature comparisons, there were 10, 10, and 30 differentially abundant proteins according to frequentist t-test, empirical Bayesian LIMMA and the random forest approach, respectively.
source: For the Young vs. Mature comparisons, there were 10, 10, and 30 differentially abundant proteins according to frequentist t-test, empirical Bayesian LIMMA and the random forest approach, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of three different statistical methods.

claim: For the Nurse vs. Forager comparison there were 21, 57, and 26 differentially abundant proteins according to frequentist t-test, empirical Bayesian LIMMA and the random forest approach, respectively.
source: Similarly, for the Nurse vs. Forager comparison there were 21, 57, and 26 differentially abundant proteins
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of three different statistical methods.

claim: When young colonies were brought to the laboratory and resampled after six months, 17, 31, or 29 proteins had significantly different abundance according to frequentist t-test, empirical Bayesian LIMMA and the random forest approach, respectively.
source: and when young colonies were brought to the laboratory and resampled after six months, 17, 31, or 29 proteins had significantly different abundance.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of three different statistical methods.

claim: The average accuracies of classification for comparisons with the random forest approach were: Young vs. Mature, 87%; Nurse vs. Forager, 93%; and Field vs. Lab, 91%.
source: The average accuracies of classification for comparisons with the random forest approach were: Young vs. Mature, 87 %; Nurse vs. Forager, 93 %; and Field vs. Lab, 91 %.
evidence: The manuscript reports the classification accuracy of the machine learning models.

claim: Young and mature colonies differed by 12 proteins when considering proteins significantly different in two out of the three forms of analysis.
source: Here, young and mature colonies differed by 12 proteins, and nurses and foragers differed by 19 proteins (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of proteins meeting the significance threshold across multiple methods.

claim: Nurses and foragers differed by 19 proteins when considering proteins significantly different in two out of the three forms of analysis.
source: Here, young and mature colonies differed by 12 proteins, and nurses and foragers differed by 19 proteins (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of proteins meeting the significance threshold across multiple methods.

claim: When young colonies were brought to the laboratory and resampled six months later, the trophallactic fluid proteomes differed significantly by 20 proteins.
source: When young colonies were brought to the laboratory and resampled six months later, the trophallactic fluid proteomes differed significantly by 20 proteins.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of proteins meeting the significance threshold across multiple methods.

claim: The 60 most abundant proteins in trophallactic fluid are predominantly involved in the biological processes of carbohydrate metabolism, lipid and sterol transport.
source: The 60 most abundant proteins in trophallactic fluid (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) are predominantly involved in the biological processes of carbohydrate metabolism, lipid and sterol transport (Figure 6, Figure 6—source data 1, FDR < 0.00038, FDR < 0.0013 and FDR < 0.0087 respectively).
evidence: The manuscript reports functional enrichment analysis results with FDR values.

claim: The larval serum protein complex was represented by three out of four members in both the most abundant proteins and in the significantly differing proteins.
source: The larval serum protein complex was represented by three out of four members in both the most abundant proteins and in the significantly differing proteins (hexamerins/arylphorins: Lsp1beta, Lsp1gamma, and Lsp2).
evidence: The manuscript identifies specific proteins from this complex in the dataset.

claim: A strong representation of the innate immune system was evident in the most abundant proteins.
source: A strong representation of the innate immune system (Reactome pathway FDR < 6.57e-5) was evident as were lysosomal processes (KEGG pathway, FDR < 3.21e-9).
evidence: The manuscript reports functional enrichment analysis results with FDR values.

claim: Lysosomal processes were evident in the most abundant proteins.
source: A strong representation of the innate immune system (Reactome pathway FDR < 6.57e-5) was evident as were lysosomal processes (KEGG pathway, FDR < 3.21e-9).
evidence: The manuscript reports functional enrichment analysis results with FDR values.

claim: Vitellogenin is the 93rd most abundant protein in trophallactic fluid, present in 77% and 88% of colony and single individual samples, respectively.
source: A critical protein in insect physiology, vitellogenin is the 93rd most abundant protein in trophallactic fluid, present in 77% and 88% of colony and single individual samples, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports the ranking and prevalence of vitellogenin in the samples.

claim: Multiple proteins of the same family were found in the most abundant trophallactic fluid proteins: a family of cathepsinD-like proteins (six in the top 60) and a family of Maltase-B1-like proteins (five in the top 60).
source: Multiple proteins of the same family were found in the most abundant trophallactic fluid proteins (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1): a family of cathepsinD-like proteins (six in the top 60; LeBoeuf et al., 2016; Hamilton et al., 2011) and a family of Maltase-B1-like proteins (five in the top 60).
evidence: The manuscript identifies protein families and their representation in the dataset.

claim: The PPI network for differentially abundant proteins was similar to that of the most abundant proteins but with increased interaction in the networks of the proteins themselves beyond what would be expected by chance.
source: The PPI network for our differentially abundant protein set (46 proteins, Figure 5) was similar to that of the most abundant proteins (Figure 4) but with increased interaction in the networks of the proteins themselves beyond what would be expected by chance (PPI enrichment p-value < 2.35e-11 in differentially abundant proteins relative to p-value < 1.59e-9 in abundant proteins)
evidence: The manuscript reports protein-protein interaction network analysis with p-values.

claim: The Nurse vs. Forager comparison yielded a network of proteins with more interaction than would have been predicted by chance.
source: The Nurse vs. Forager comparison yielded a network of proteins with more interaction than would have been predicted by chance (PPI enrichment p-value < 2.57e-4) as well as a higher degree of PPI enrichment than the other two comparisons (Young vs. Mature p < 0.002 and Field v Lab p < 0.02).
evidence: The manuscript reports protein-protein interaction network analysis with p-values.

claim: The orthologs of differentially abundant proteins found in the behavioral caste comparison involved carbohydrate processing, oxidation-reduction and malate metabolic processes.
source: The orthologs of differentially abundant proteins found in the behavioral caste comparison involved not only carbohydrate processing (FDR < 1.7e-4), but also oxidation-reduction and malate metabolic processes (FDR < 0.023 and FDR < 0.02, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript reports functional enrichment analysis results with FDR values.

claim: Two of the 46 differentially abundant proteins over all comparisons have D. melanogaster orthologs with the gene ontology term 'determination of adult lifespan'.
source: Indeed, two of the 46 differentially abundant proteins over all comparisons have D. melanogaster orthologs with the gene ontology term 'determination of adult lifespan' (Men, Sod1).
evidence: The manuscript identifies specific proteins with this GO term annotation.

claim: The random forest classifier assigned an average out-of-box maturity score to laboratory samples of 42% mature, reflecting the intermediate position of the laboratory colony samples.
source: Our random forest classifier assigned an average out-of-box maturity score to our 16 laboratory samples of 42 % mature, reflecting the intermediate position of the laboratory colony samples in Figure 3.
evidence: The manuscript reports the classification results of the machine learning model.

claim: Trophallactic fluid includes many enzymes involved in metabolism and protein products of metabolism.
source: We found that trophallactic fluid includes many enzymes involved in metabolism and protein products of metabolism.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from proteomic analysis.

claim: Proteins abundant in mature colonies (Lsps, apolpp) are major insect nutrient storage proteins that may be required to consolidate resources into large workers and sexuals, potentially acting as superorganismal hormones.
source: Some proteins abundant in mature colonies (Lsps, apolpp Burmester and Scheller, 1999; Burmester, 2002; Burmester, 1999) are major insect nutrient storage proteins (Burmester, 1999) that may be required to consolidate resources into large workers and sexuals, potentially acting as superorganismal hormones.
evidence: The manuscript combines data from this study with cited literature and proposes a functional role.

claim: Proteins abundant in foragers and young colonies (Gld, tobi, Amy, Mal) are well-conserved enzymes for fast sugar processing.
source: Proteins abundant in foragers and young colonies (Gld, tobi, Amy, Mal, Buch et al., 2008; White et al., 2021) are well-conserved enzymes for fast sugar processing.
evidence: The manuscript combines data from this study with cited literature to characterize these proteins.

claim: Trophallactic fluid transmits numerous factors linked to ageing and coping with oxidative stress, including two of the three most well-known antioxidant enzymes: superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase.
source: We show that trophallactic fluid transmits numerous factors linked to ageing and coping with oxidative stress, including two of the three most well-known antioxidant enzymes: superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase (Monaghan et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript reports identification of these proteins in trophallactic fluid and cites literature on their function.

claim: Ageing-related proteins, such as those in redox pathways and malate metabolism, are especially elevated in nurses.
source: These and other ageing-related proteins, such as those in redox pathways and malate metabolism (Wiley and Campisi, 2016; Koch et al., 2021), are especially elevated in nurses, the individuals that are physically the closest to the brood and queen in the trophallactic network.
evidence: The manuscript reports differential protein abundance and cites literature on protein function.

claim: If molecules dealing with oxidative stress, or beneficial products of metabolism can be spread over the circulatory system, certain individuals may bear the costs that others in the network incur.
source: If molecules dealing with oxidative stress, or beneficial products of metabolism (nutrient storage proteins) can be spread over the circulatory system, as our results show, certain individuals may bear the costs that others in the network incur.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanism based on the observed protein distributions.

claim: Gene-set enrichment analysis showed significant enrichment in immunity-related proteins characteristic of phagocytic hemocytes in trophallactic fluid.
source: Our gene-set enrichment analysis showed significant enrichment in immunity-related proteins characteristic of phagocytic hemocytes (Shokal and Eleftherianos, 2017) in trophallactic fluid ('innate immune system', 'complement cascade', 'neutrophil degranulation').
evidence: The manuscript reports functional enrichment analysis results and cites literature on hemocyte characteristics.

claim: These results indicate that hemocytes may themselves be transmitted mouth-to-mouth.
source: These results indicate that hemocytes may themselves be transmitted mouth-to-mouth, and generally shows the involvement of the social circulatory system in colony-level immune responses with implications for social immunity.
evidence: The manuscript infers this possibility from the presence of hemocyte-characteristic proteins.

claim: Lysosomal pathways are enriched in the most abundant trophallactic fluid proteins and in the set of significantly varying trophallactic fluid proteins between nurses and foragers.
source: Lysosomal pathways are enriched in our most abundant trophallactic fluid proteins and in our set of significantly varying trophallactic fluid proteins between nurses and foragers, according to the KEGG analysis.
evidence: The manuscript reports functional enrichment analysis results.

claim: As trophallactic fluid has become acidified in formicine ants, lysosomal genes could have been duplicated and neofunctionalized to a new role in this acidic fluid, similarly to juvenile-hormone-esterase-like proteins in trophallactic fluid.
source: As trophallactic fluid has become acidified in formicine ants (Tragust et al., 2020), lysosomal genes could have been duplicated and neofunctionalized to a new role in this acidic fluid, similarly to juvenile-hormone-esterase-like proteins in trophallactic fluid (LeBoeuf et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript proposes an evolutionary mechanism based on cited literature and observed protein families.

claim: Camponotus floridanus is a common species of carpenter ant in the south-eastern USA.
source: Camponotus floridanus is a common species of carpenter ant in the south-eastern USA, and has already been the focus of previous trophallactic fluid analyses (LeBoeuf et al., 2016; LeBoeuf et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about the study species.

claim: Each C. floridanus colony has a single, singly mated queen.
source: Each colony has a single, singly mated queen (Gadau et al., 1996), and polydomous nest-structures where queenless satellite nests are common.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statement about colony structure.

claim: C. floridanus colonies grow to tens of thousands of workers and produce sexual brood only after multiple years of initial growth.
source: Colonies grow to tens of thousands of workers and produce sexual brood only after multiple years of initial growth.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about the species.

claim: Large established C. floridanus colonies have two morphologically differentiated worker castes, with variably sized small-headed minors focusing on brood care when young and foraging when old, and big-headed majors that engage in nest defense, foraging and food storage.
source: Large established colonies have two morphologically differentiated worker castes, with variably sized small-headed minors focusing on brood care when young and foraging when old, and big-headed majors that engage in nest defense, foraging and food storage (Deyrup, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this description of worker castes.

claim: A colony was deemed 'young' if the worker population was <100, primarily minors, and the queen was found.
source: A colony was deemed 'young' if the worker population was <100, primarily minors, and the queen was found (meaning both that the species could be clearly identified and that the nest was not a queenless satellite of an established colony)
evidence: The manuscript defines the criteria used for classifying colonies in this study.

claim: A colony was deemed 'mature' if the colony was larger (>1000 individuals visible) and the opened nest contained many large aggressive majors.
source: and 'mature' if the colony was larger ( > 1000 individuals visible) and the opened nest contained many large aggressive majors.
evidence: The manuscript defines the criteria used for classifying colonies in this study.

claim: Young C. floridanus colonies lack majors.
source: Young colonies lack majors (Gibson, 1989) and individuals are generally less aggressive.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this observation.

claim: Trophallactic fluid was obtained from CO2- or cold-anesthetized workers whose abdomens were gently squeezed to force them to regurgitate the contents of their crops.
source: Trophallactic fluid was obtained from CO2- or cold-anesthetized workers whose abdomens were gently squeezed to force them to regurgitate the contents of their crops.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental method used.

claim: This method of collection was shown previously to correspond to the fluid shared during the act of adult-adult stomodeal trophallaxis.
source: This method of collection was shown previously to correspond to the fluid shared during the act of adult-adult stomodeal trophallaxis (LeBoeuf et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to validate the collection method.

claim: For each colony, at least 30 individuals were sampled to obtain at least 10 µl of raw trophallactic fluid.
source: For each colony, at least 30 individuals were sampled to obtain at least 10 µl of raw trophallactic fluid.
evidence: The manuscript describes the sampling protocol used.

claim: The total proteomics sample number is 73 colony samples and 40 individual samples.
source: The total proteomics sample number is 73 colony samples of following types: 23 mature colonies with two of them sampled six times, 20 young colonies in the field, 16 young colonies in the laboratory, four laboratory colonies used for single individual sampling; and 40 individual samples: 20 nurses and 20 foragers.
evidence: The manuscript reports the total sample sizes for the study.

claim: The MS raw data files were uploaded into MaxQuant software, version 1.6.2.10, for peak detection, generation of peak lists of mass error corrected peptides, and for database searches.
source: The MS raw data files were uploaded into MaxQuant software (Tyanova et al., 2016a), version 1.6.2.10, for peak detection, generation of peak lists of mass error corrected peptides, and for database searches.
evidence: The manuscript describes the data analysis method used.

claim: MaxQuant was set up to search both the UniProt and NCBI databases restricted to C. floridanus.
source: MaxQuant was set up to search both the UniProt (RRID:SCR_002380, https://www.uniprot.org/) and NCBI (RRID:SCR_003496, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) databases restricted to C. floridanus (UniProt, February 2020 version; NCBI RefSeq, version 7.5), along with common contaminants, such as keratins and enzymes used for digestion.
evidence: The manuscript describes the database search parameters used.

claim: After filtering, the dataset contained 519 proteins.
source: All proteins labelled as contaminants, reverse or only identified by site were excluded and proteins with scores less than 70 were removed. After the filtering, the dataset contained 519 proteins.
evidence: The manuscript reports the final number of proteins after quality filtering.

claim: Quantitative analysis was performed using iBAQ values.
source: Quantitative analysis was performed using iBAQ values. Intensity-based absolute quantification (iBAQ) is the quotient of sum of all identified peptides and the number of theoretically observable peptides of a protein (Schwanhäusser et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript describes the quantification method used and cites the original publication.

claim: The protein composition of ant trophallactic fluid varies across different external contexts and internal conditions both at the colony and at the individual level.
source: We show that the protein composition of ant trophallactic fluid varies across different external contexts and internal conditions both at the colony and at the individual level, suggesting that the dynamic trophallactic fluid proteome has key functions in social physiology and life cycle of colonies.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: The dynamic trophallactic fluid proteome has key functions in social physiology and life cycle of colonies.
source: We show that the protein composition of ant trophallactic fluid varies across different external contexts and internal conditions both at the colony and at the individual level, suggesting that the dynamic trophallactic fluid proteome has key functions in social physiology and life cycle of colonies.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this functional role based on the observed variation.

claim: The overall protein abundance was higher in colony samples relative to single individual samples, reflective of the larger trophallactic fluid volume collected.
source: The overall protein abundance was higher in colony samples relative to single individual samples, reflective of the larger trophallactic fluid volume collected.
evidence: The manuscript explains the difference in protein abundance between sample types.

claim: Protein abundance did not correlate with the proportion of samples containing the protein across the entire dataset.
source: Even though the most common proteins displayed higher average abundance, across the entire dataset, protein abundance did not correlate with the proportion of samples containing the protein – even proteins present in only a small proportion of the samples in some cases exhibited high abundance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the lack of correlation between abundance and prevalence.

claim: The trophallactic proteome variability of young and mature colonies did not differ significantly.
source: The trophallactic proteome variability of young and mature colonies did not differ significantly, nor did nurses' and foragers' (Figure 2b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of statistical comparison.

claim: The trophallactic proteome variability of nurses and foragers did not differ significantly.
source: The trophallactic proteome variability of young and mature colonies did not differ significantly, nor did nurses' and foragers' (Figure 2b).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of statistical comparison.

claim: The frequentist analysis between different sampling areas found no significantly different proteins.
source: The frequentist analysis between different sampling areas found no significantly different proteins, and the random forest model did not reach high enough accuracy for this dataset to be informative (58 % classification accuracy).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of statistical analysis for spatial comparison.

claim: The random forest model for East vs. West comparison did not reach high enough accuracy to be informative (58% classification accuracy).
source: The frequentist analysis between different sampling areas found no significantly different proteins, and the random forest model did not reach high enough accuracy for this dataset to be informative (58 % classification accuracy).
evidence: The manuscript reports the classification accuracy of the machine learning model.

claim: Only the empirical Bayes approach found eight proteins that significantly differed between the sampling areas.
source: Only the empirical Bayes approach found eight proteins that significantly differed between the sampling areas (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary files 2 and 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of the empirical Bayes analysis.

claim: The single individual dataset showed that proteomes are affected both by colony of origin and by behavioral role of the individual, with 60 proteins showing significant interaction between the two factors.
source: Additionally, the single individual dataset showed that proteomes are affected both by colony of origin and by behavioral role of the individual, with 60 proteins showing significant interaction between the two factors (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of two-way ANOVA analysis.

claim: Three of the 60 most abundant proteins had no similarity to Drosophila genes.
source: Three of the 60 most abundant proteins had no similarity to Drosophila genes, and thus could not be included in the functional enrichment analysis.
evidence: The manuscript reports the orthology analysis results.

claim: One of the three proteins with no similarity to Drosophila genes is a putative odorant receptor.
source: One of them is a putative odorant receptor, another a G-protein alpha subunit, and the third showed no orthology to characterized proteins.
evidence: The manuscript reports the annotation of proteins without Drosophila orthologs.

claim: There was an overlap of 16 proteins between the most abundant proteins and the proteins significant in two out of three of the statistical methods in any of the comparisons.
source: There was an overlap of 16 proteins between the most abundant proteins and the proteins significant in two out of three of our statistical methods in any of the comparisons.
evidence: The manuscript reports the overlap between different protein sets.

claim: The differentially abundant protein set showed noted enrichment in oxidation-reduction processes and stronger enrichment in carbohydrate metabolic processes.
source: The PPI network for our differentially abundant protein set (46 proteins, Figure 5) was similar to that of the most abundant proteins (Figure 4) but with increased interaction in the networks of the proteins themselves beyond what would be expected by chance (PPI enrichment p-value < 2.35e-11 in differentially abundant proteins relative to p-value < 1.59e-9 in abundant proteins), with noted enrichment in oxidation-reduction processes (FDR < 0.0026) and stronger enrichment in carbohydrate metabolic processes (FDR < 2.15e-6).
evidence: The manuscript reports functional enrichment analysis results with FDR values.

claim: The C. floridanus tetraspanin, significantly more abundant in nurse trophallactic fluid, is a one-to-many ortholog to the family of Tsp42E genes, one of which has been implicated in determination of adult lifespan in D. melanogaster.
source: The C. floridanus tetraspanin, significantly more abundant in nurse trophallactic fluid, is a one-to-many ortholog to the family of Tsp42E genes, one of which has also been implicated in determination of adult lifespan in D. melanogaster.
evidence: The manuscript reports orthology and functional annotation of this protein.

claim: Trophallactic fluid complexity declines over time when colonies are brought from the field to the laboratory.
source: At the individual level, certain trophallactic fluid proteins correlate with behavioral caste within the colony, a trait known to encompass both individual task requirements and age (Korb et al., 2021; Mersch et al., 2013; Wild et al., 2021). Trophallactic fluid complexity declines over time when colonies are brought from the field to the laboratory.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a finding from the Field vs. Lab comparison.

claim: The decline in trophallactic fluid complexity in laboratory colonies may reflect dietary, microbiome or environmental complexity.
source: This may reflect dietary, microbiome or environmental complexity – typical of traits that have evolved to deal with environmental cues and stressors (e.g. immunity, Lazzaro and Little, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript proposes possible explanations for the observed decline and cites relevant literature.

claim: Similar shifts in protein composition or gene expression can be seen in different tissues of multicellular organisms as life-stage priorities change, for example in the midgut of drosophila females after mating.
source: Similar shifts in protein composition or gene expression can be seen in different tissues of multicellular organisms as life-stage priorities change, for example in the midgut of drosophila females after mating, where changes in expression are observed in many genes orthologous to the proteins we found here (White et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to draw parallels with other biological systems.

claim: Drosophila larval hemolymph proteome changes as development unfolds, and many of these same proteins also appear in the comparisons of worker trophallactic fluid.
source: Additionally, Drosophila larval hemolymph proteome changes as development unfolds (Handke et al., 2013), and many of these same proteins also appear in our comparisons of worker trophallactic fluid.
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature and notes overlap with proteins found in this study.

claim: Regulation of larval development may at least in part occur over the social network of ants.
source: We suggest that regulation of larval development may at least in part occur over the social network of ants, in line with previous experimental results (LeBoeuf et al., 2018).
